title: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field: Examples and Applications
short: Force on a Moving Charge: Applications
lead: A magnetic force always acts at right angles to the velocity of the charge it acts on, and a force like that can never speed a particle up or slow it down. All it can do is turn it, and a force of constant size that keeps turning a particle at right angles to its motion is exactly what uniform circular motion asks for. This section works out how wide that circle is, finding that the radius is the mass times the speed divided by the charge times the field strength, and then tips the velocity out of the plane so that the circle becomes a spiral running along a field line. That is enough to account for the curved tracks in a bubble chamber, the spiral a magnet makes of the electrons in a television tube, the aurora, the belts of trapped particles above the atmosphere, and the fields built on purpose to hold a beam or a plasma where it is wanted.
objectives: Describe the effects of a magnetic field on a moving charge.
Calculate the radius of curvature of the path of a charge that is moving in a magnetic field.
summary_html: • Magnetic force can supply centripetal force and cause a charged particle to move in a circular path of radius$$\kr = \frac{m\kv}{\kq\kBmag},$$where $\kv$ is the component of the velocity perpendicular to $\kBmag$ for a charged particle with mass m and charge q.
notes: Six problems are left out. Five of them the book leaves without an answer: the field strength that holds a proton in a 0.800 m circle, the charge on an oxygen-16 ion, the field and voltage of a velocity selector, the four comparisons between a proton and an electron, and the separation of the uranium isotopes. The sixth, which asks for the radius an electron would travel in the same field as that proton, goes with it, since the book leaves the proton’s field unanswered and the question cannot be read without it. The section’s one test prep item asks for the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire, so it is set in Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor, which introduces that force.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 22.18) Trails of bubbles are produced by high-energy charged particles moving through the superheated liquid hydrogen in this artist’s rendition of a bubble chamber. There is a strong magnetic field perpendicular to the page that causes the curved paths of the particles. The radius of the path can be used to find the mass, charge, and energy of the particle. (Figure 22.19) A negatively charged particle moves in the plane of the page in a region where the magnetic field is perpendicular into the page (represented by the small circles with x’s—like the tails of arrows). The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, and so velocity changes in direction but not magnitude. Uniform circular motion results.

(Figure 22.20) Side view showing what happens when a magnet comes in contact with a computer monitor or TV screen. Electrons moving toward the screen spiral about magnetic field lines, maintaining the component of their velocity parallel to the field lines. This distorts the image on the screen. (Figure 22.21) When a charged particle moves along a magnetic field line into a region where the field becomes stronger, the particle experiences a force that reduces the component of velocity parallel to the field. This force slows the motion along the field line and here reverses it, forming a “magnetic mirror.”

(Figure 22.22) Energetic electrons and protons, components of cosmic rays, from the Sun and deep outer space often follow the Earth’s magnetic field lines rather than cross them. (Recall that the Earth’s north magnetic pole is really a south pole in terms of a bar magnet.) (Figure 22.23) The Van Allen radiation belts are two regions in which energetic charged particles are trapped in the Earth’s magnetic field. One belt lies about 300 km above the Earth’s surface, the other about 16,000 km. Charged particles in these belts migrate along magnetic field lines and are partially reflected away from the poles by the stronger fields there. The charged particles that enter the atmosphere are replenished by the Sun and sources in deep outer space.

exercises.prompt: How can the motion of a charged particle be used to distinguish between a magnetic and an electric field?

answer.solution: Watch what happens to the speed. An electric field exerts a force $\kq\kEf$ along the field itself, whatever the charge is doing, so it can act along the direction of motion and change the speed; a charge released at rest in an electric field is set moving in a straight line. A magnetic field exerts a force $\kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta$ that is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work, leaves the kinetic energy and the speed unchanged, and only turns the path; a charge at rest in a magnetic field feels no force at all, and a charge moving across the field travels a circle at constant speed. So a particle that speeds up or slows down in a straight line has met an electric field, and one that keeps its speed and bends into a circle or a spiral has met a magnetic one.

exercises.prompt: High-velocity charged particles can damage biological cells and are a component of radiation exposure in a variety of locations ranging from research facilities to natural background. Describe how you could use a magnetic field to shield yourself.

answer.solution: Surround the space to be protected with a magnetic field whose lines run across the direction the particles come from. A charged particle that has to cross the field lines is bent into a circle of radius $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$, so if the field is strong enough that this radius is small compared with the thickness of the field region, the particle is turned right round before it can get through and never reaches you. That is exactly what the Earth does at middle latitudes, where incoming cosmic rays must cross the field lines and many of them are prevented from reaching the atmosphere. The shield is least effective along the direction of the field itself, since a particle traveling along a field line feels no force, so the field has to be arranged to leave no such path open.

exercises.prompt: If a cosmic ray proton approaches the Earth from outer space along a line toward the center of the Earth that lies in the plane of the equator, in what direction will it be deflected by the Earth’s magnetic field? What about an electron? A neutron?

answer.solution: Over the equator the Earth’s field points north, and the proton is traveling inward, that is, downward toward the center. Right hand rule 1 with the fingers on the velocity and curled toward the field puts the force on a positive charge toward the east, so the proton is deflected east. The electron carries the opposite sign, so the same rule gives the opposite direction and it is deflected west. The neutron has no charge, and the magnetic force on a charge is proportional to that charge, so the neutron feels no magnetic force at all and carries straight on.

figure.alt: Diagram showing magnetic field lines into the page. Charges are moving from the bottom to the top of the diagram and thus perpendicular to the field lines. Charge a curves to the left. Charge b moves in a straight line from bottom to top. Charge c curves to the right.

exercises.prompt: What are the signs of the charges on the particles in the figure below?

answer.solution: The field is into the page and all three particles move up the page. Right hand rule 1 for a positive charge moving up across a field into the page gives a force to the left, so the particle that curves to the left, particle a, is positive. Particle c curves to the right, the opposite way, so it carries a negative charge. Particle b is not deflected at all, and since the speed and the field are the same for all three, the only way to feel no magnetic force is to carry no charge: particle b is neutral.

figure.alt: Diagram showing magnetic field lines out of the page. Charge a curves clockwise with a large radius as it moves from the bottom to the top of the diagram. Charge b curves clockwise with a much smaller radius as it moves from lower middle to upper middle of the diagram.

exercises.prompt: Which of the particles in the figure below has the greatest velocity, assuming they have identical charges and masses?

answer.solution: Particle a, the one on the wider arc. The radius of the circle is $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$, so with the same mass, the same charge and the same field, the radius is proportional to the speed. The particle whose path curves least is therefore the fastest one.

figure.alt: Diagram showing magnetic field lines out of the page. Charge a curves clockwise with a large radius as it moves from the bottom to the top of the diagram. Charge b curves clockwise with a much smaller radius as it moves from lower middle to upper middle of the diagram.

exercises.prompt: Which of the particles in the figure above has the greatest mass, assuming all have identical charges and velocities?

answer.solution: Particle a again, for the same reason read the other way. In $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$ the radius is proportional to the mass when the speed, the charge and the field are held fixed, so the heavier particle is the one that swings round the wider arc. This is what a mass spectrometer measures: fix the speed, the charge and the field, and the radius of the path is a reading of the mass.

exercises.prompt: While operating, a high-precision TV monitor is placed on its side during maintenance. The image on the monitor changes color and blurs slightly. Discuss the possible relation of these effects to the Earth’s magnetic field.

answer.solution: The picture is painted by electrons crossing the tube, and the Earth’s field bends them into arcs of radius $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$ just as a magnet held against the glass does, though far more gently because the Earth’s field is some ten thousand times weaker than a permanent magnet’s. What matters is that only the component of the velocity perpendicular to the field is bent. Standing the monitor on its side turns the electron beams with respect to the Earth’s field, so that component changes, and the beams land in slightly different places than they did before. Since the three colors are produced by three beams that must strike their own phosphor dots, a small shift blurs the image and misregisters the colors.

exercises.prompt: A cosmic ray electron moves at $7.50 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$ perpendicular to the Earth’s magnetic field at an altitude where field strength is $1.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. What is the radius of the circular path the electron follows?

answer.hint: The radius of the path is $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$. Put in the mass of the electron, $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, and its charge, $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C, along with the speed and the field strength given.

exercises.prompt: (a) Viewers of Star Trek hear of an antimatter drive on the Starship Enterprise. One possibility for such a futuristic energy source is to store antimatter charged particles in a vacuum chamber, circulating in a magnetic field, and then extract them as needed. Antimatter annihilates with normal matter, producing pure energy. What strength magnetic field is needed to hold antiprotons, moving at $5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$ in a circular path 2.00 m in radius? Antiprotons have the same mass as protons but the opposite (negative) charge. (b) Is this field strength obtainable with today’s technology or is it a futuristic possibility?

parts.hint: Solve $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$ for the field, $\kBmag = m\kv/\kq\kr$. The antiproton has the mass of a proton, $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, and a charge of the same size as the electron’s.

answer.solution: (a) 0.261 T. (b) This strength is definitely obtainable with today’s technology. Magnetic field strengths of 0.500 T are obtainable with permanent magnets.

exercises.prompt: An electron in a TV CRT moves with a speed of $6.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$, in a direction perpendicular to the Earth’s field, which has a strength of $5.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. (a) What strength electric field must be applied perpendicular to the Earth’s field to make the electron moves in a straight line? (b) If this is done between plates separated by 1.00 cm, what is the voltage applied? (Note that TVs are usually surrounded by a ferromagnetic material to shield against external magnetic fields and avoid the need for such a correction.)

parts.hint: For the path to stay straight the electric force must balance the magnetic force, so $\kq\kEf = \kq\kv\kBmag$ and the charge cancels.
Between parallel plates the field is the voltage divided by the separation, so the voltage is the field strength times 1.00 cm.

exercises.prompt: A mass spectrometer is being used to separate common oxygen-16 from the much rarer oxygen-18, taken from a sample of old glacial ice. (The relative abundance of these oxygen isotopes is related to climatic temperature at the time the ice was deposited.) The ratio of the masses of these two ions is 16 to 18, the mass of oxygen-16 is $2.66 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg},$ and they are singly charged and travel at $5.00 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$ in a 1.20-T magnetic field. What is the separation between their paths when they hit a target after traversing a semicircle?

answer.hint: Each ion travels a half circle, so it lands a distance $2\kr$ from where it entered. Work out $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$ for each mass and take twice the difference between the two radii.
